AMD Stock Dropped 11% Last Week. Is Intel's PC Warning Really That Bad? ©@undefined from Getty Images Pro via Canva, @Kittipong Jirasukhanont from PhonlamaiPhoto's Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) stock declined approximately 11% from October 30 to November 6, closing near $449 as semiconductor valuations came under pressure.

Intel (INTC) warned that PC weakness could extend into 2027, while AMD's third-quarter data center revenue surged 97% to $8.5 billion.

AMD expects approximately $17 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, but its premium valuation leaves limited room for weaker earnings growth.

What Happened?

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) stock dropped approximately 11% from October 30 to November 6, closing near $449 as investors weighed weakening PC demand against AMD's accelerating AI infrastructure growth.

Intel's October 29 earnings report added to concerns about semiconductor demand, with fourth-quarter revenue guidance of $15 billion to $16 billion and a warning that PC weakness could continue into 2027.

Intel CFO David Zinsner said, "we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," highlighting continued uncertainty across consumer computing markets.

However, AMD's November 3 earnings report presented a stronger picture of semiconductor demand.

The company reported third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% year over year, while adjusted earnings per share climbed 74% to $2.09.

Data center revenue surged 97% to $8.5 billion, driven by strong demand for AMD Instinct GPUs and EPYC server processors.

AMD also projected approximately $17 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, representing 66% annual growth at the midpoint.

Despite those results, shares remained volatile, falling 17% on November 5 before rebounding 11% on November 6 as investors reassessed semiconductor valuations.

Intel's PC Warning Is a Smaller Problem for AMD

Intel's warning remains relevant because AMD still has meaningful exposure to consumer and commercial PC markets.

AMD's third-quarter client revenue increased 7% to $2.9 billion, although its broader Client and Gaming segment declined 8% to $3.7 billion.

However, data center revenue represented approximately 64% of AMD's quarterly sales, making AI infrastructure considerably more important to its overall growth.

Intel's data center and AI revenue increased 78% to $7.3 billion, demonstrating continued enterprise demand for server processors despite weaker PC conditions.

Intel also acknowledged supply constraints affecting its ability to meet strong Xeon demand, potentially creating opportunities for AMD to expand its EPYC server business.

AMD's growing AI partnerships, including Helios rack-scale systems installed and undergoing testing at Meta, further support its long-term growth prospects.

title: AMD Stock Has More Than Doubled in 2026. Here's How Its Last 8 Doubles Played Out the Next Year.
detail:
AMD Stock Has More Than Doubled in 2026. Here's How Its Last 8 Doubles Played Out the Next Year.

Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) shareholders are having a huge year. Trading around $486 as of this writing, the shares are up about 127% in 2026, on top of a 77% gain in 2025.

The company has kept up, too. AMD's third-quarter revenue grew to a record $13.4 billion, a 45% rise from the year-ago quarter, as data center sales almost doubled.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But a year like this isn't new to AMD. Going by year-end closing prices since 1981, the shares at least doubled in eight other calendar years. And the year after split evenly with four gains and four losses.

What does that record tell someone thinking about buying the shares now?

Image source: AMD.

Four up, four down

AMD's eight earlier double years are in the table, each beside the stock's price change in the following year. AMD has never paid a cash dividend, so every price change is the total return.

Year

Price change the next year

Data source: Yahoo Finance. Calculations by author.

Put simply, investors learned nearly nothing about the next year's direction from a double. AMD rose in 21 of the 45 full calendar years from 1981 through 2025, or around 47% of the time. After a double, it rose in four of eight. Either way, the odds were near a coin flip.

And 2020 almost made the list itself. The shares climbed just under 100% that year, then added another 57% in 2021.

The average follow-up year was far better than the split suggests, with a gain of around 33%. But that average leans on two years, 1983 and 2020, with gains of about 168% and 100%. The other six follow-up years averaged a small loss.

The losing years were mild

I think the more useful pattern is in the size of the losses. All four of AMD's down years after a double were fairly modest, ranging from a 9% decline in 2017 to an 18% drop in 2024.

A bad year for this growth stock normally looks far worse. AMD fell in 24 of its 45 full calendar years, and its typical decline in those years was around 31%. In 14 of the 24, it lost over 20%, including a 71% drop in 2008 and a 55% slide in 2022.

So, an investor who owned AMD heading into any of the double years kept most of the gain through the next year. The worst case was 2023 to 2024, when a 128% gain was followed by an 18% drop. Someone who held through both years still had around 86% more money than at the start.

Key Takeaways

Broadcom fell 15.5% in the week to Nov. 5 as Intel's weak outlook and fears of tighter AI rules hit chip stocks, Nvidia and AMD included.

The bigger risk is Broadcom's own: it backstops up to about $72 billion of financing for AI racks leased to Anthropic.

The stock trades well below its usual forward P/E, and its December report is the next test.

Broadcom (AVGO:NASDAQ) fell 15.5% in the week to Nov. 5 with no news of its own. Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) started a chip rout with a weak outlook, and fears of tighter AI rules after the midterms deepened it, dragging down Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) too.

Intel lit the fuse

Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion after the Oct. 29 close, short of the roughly $17 billion analysts expected. Broadcom lost 5.5% on Oct. 30, while Intel fell 28.6% and went on to lose 43.2% in the week to Nov. 5.

Democrats then won both chambers of Congress on Nov. 3. Chip stocks slid on Nov. 4, then plunged on Nov. 5 on worries about slower data center building, with Broadcom down 10.4% that day.

Nvidia fell 15.0% in the week, about as much as Broadcom. AMD lost 28.6%, even though its forecast after the Nov. 3 close called for about $17 billion of fourth-quarter revenue, above the roughly $16.2 billion analysts expected.

Nothing changed at Broadcom

In its fiscal third quarter, revenue rose 86% to $29.6 billion, and AI chip revenue jumped 221% to $16.7 billion. Committed contract value hit $179.2 billion at Aug. 2, and management is aiming for about $115 billion of AI revenue in fiscal 2027.

Power was already the bottleneck: CEO Hock Tan called land, power and the building shell "more than a big concern" on the third-quarter call. Tighter rules could make that worse, but the orders are already on the books.

Analysts expect normalized EPS of $11.67 for the fiscal year that ended Nov. 1, up about 70% from $6.82 in fiscal 2025, and $30.37 by fiscal 2028:

title: Bank of America has unexpected advice for tech stock investors after midterms
detail:
Bank of America has unexpected advice for tech stock investors after midterms
Moz Farooque, Aparajita Chatterjee

^NDX

NVDA

Checking your retirement account on Thursday afternoon, November 5, felt like a gut punch, with months of hard-earned gains vanishing in hours. 

Even with diversification in mind, simply holding a standard index fund left you absorbing the damage. The Nasdaq 100 erased $2.3 trillion in market value as a post-midterm panic triggered a brutal tech sell-off, Bloomberg reported. 

AI poster-children like Nvidia tumbled more than 9%, while AMD plunged over 17%. The bounce-back the next day brought brief relief but zero answers.

For years, riding Big Tech felt like a foolproof ticket to America's AI boom. Now, mounting political resistance to data centers and runaway corporate spending have investors asking if the math has permanently changed.

Bank of America has a surprising answer. Its post-election outlook uncovers a contrarian opportunity, posing an urgent question for anyone counting on the stock market for retirement.

Why Bank of America favors tech debt over tech stocks

Bank of America just dropped one of the most surprising messages for investors rattled by tech's sell-off: that owning a great tech business isn't necessarily the best way to invest in it. For now, the bank prefers tech company bonds to tech stocks.

More Wall Street:

Nvidia and Micron are about to lord their successes all over Wall Street

Nvidia, Palantir and Alphabet send waves through Wall Street

Wall Street elites will pocket windfall from record $46 billion profits

In post-midterm research, chief investment strategist Michael Hartnett favored "tech bonds over tech stocks," as reported by Seeking Alpha. Bonds pay contractual interest and generally rank ahead of common shares if a company fails. That said, they aren't risk-free, and missed payments and rising market yields can still hurt investors.

The shift goes further. BofA prefers consumer staples, represented by the Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLP), to energy shares represented by XLE. It also favors smaller businesses over market giants as reported by TipRanks.

That's meaningful for retirement savers. An S&P 500 fund owns hundreds of stocks, but its largest holdings carry outsized weight, a concentration risk that veteran market commentator Jim Cramer has also warned about.

After years when giant technology firms led returns, a pullback in just a few companies can affect an otherwise diversified account.

BofA strategists raised the possibility of "peak AI equity concentration," questioning where the next dollar of investment belongs.

Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) lost about 17% of their value in one session on Thursday, Nov. 5, closing at $404.40. The company itself didn't announce anything new that day.

Instead, chip stocks sold off across the board as election wins by candidates who vowed to limit artificial intelligence (AI) data centers fueled rising worries about the AI boom. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 12.3%, its worst day since March 2020.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

After AMD's third-quarter results on Nov. 3, I wrote that I'd consider buying the stock if it traded around $480. That price was 30 times the non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share analysts expect AMD to post in 2027 on average, which is about $16. Thursday's close is around 16% below it.

What changed between Tuesday night and Thursday's close? As far as I can see, just the share price did.

Image source: AMD.

AMD's 2027 outlook hasn't changed

Even after Thursday's fall, AMD stock is up around 89% in 2026. But it's also about 38% off the all-time high close it set on Oct. 6 ($649.42) -- lots of ground to give up in a month.

Meanwhile, the business is speeding up. Showing how much demand there is for its data center chips, AMD's third-quarter revenue rose 45% from a year earlier to a record $13.4 billion. AMD is guiding for around $17 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, about 66% more than in the same period of 2025.

And on the Nov. 3 earnings call, CEO Lisa Su said AMD now expects revenue to rise over 80% in 2027. Put another way, growth is accelerating, from 45% in the third quarter to around 66% in the fourth and more than 80% for 2027 overall.

Might the political worry in Thursday's sell-off hold that back? An analyst asked Su on the call about the land and power behind next year's ramp.

"We have been planning for this ramp with our customers jointly. So we have good visibility into 2027 ... land, power, shell, all of those, the data center infrastructure," Su said.

Simply put, the data centers AMD's chips are going to next year seem mostly planned already. Tighter rules for new construction could matter more for 2028 and later than for 2027.

A $16 year looks reachable

The $16 estimate is worth checking against AMD's own numbers. In the first nine months of 2026, the company's adjusted earnings per share were $5.12. Management's fourth-quarter guidance for revenue, margins and expenses implies about $2.90 more, for about $8 this year. Reaching $16 would mean a doubling.

AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) reported third-quarter earnings on Nov. 3, and the stock rose sharply after hours, up around 8%. However, over the next day, the market was less and less impressed with the results, and AMD ended Nov. 4 up only about 1% -- less than the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) rose. So, what caused the market to change its mind after a strong reaction?

I think investors are looking at AMD as a whole, rather than just a single quarter.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The reality is that AMD's stock has risen tremendously fast this year, far outpacing its business growth. This mismatch has vaulted AMD's stock into expensive territory, and that reality is apparently becoming clear to investors.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
AMD sees strong data center growth ahead

First, let's digest the quarter. AMD makes all types of computing units, ranging from data center GPUs to consumer hardware to embedded chip processors. However, the big cash cow is its data center business, which is growing rapidly. During Q3, AMD's data center business rose 97% year over year to $8.5 billion. However, this still represents a slowdown from the 107% growth seen in Q2. Furthermore, data centers are only a part of AMD's business. AMD's overall revenue totaled $13.4 billion, up 45% year over year. So, AMD is being held back by its other business units.

Looking ahead, AMD expects strong growth. It expects data center revenue to double year over year in 2027 -- indicating that its growth in this area will remain strong. That's great news for investors, as it suggests AMD's overall growth rate will likely increase. With its data center division growing faster than the company overall, it will start to make up an ever larger share of AMD's total. With it having a greater effect, AMD's overall growth rate will move closer to the data center unit's.

This is great news, but it's also required, as AMD's stock has a lot of future growth priced in.

AMD isn't a cheap stock

Right now, AMD is one of the more expensive stocks on the market.

AMD PE Ratio data by YCharts

Priced at 106 times trailing earnings, AMD's stock is expensive no matter how you slice it. The company needs to grow its way into a more reasonable valuation. One way AMD is doing this is by improving margins. Each quarter over the past few years, AMD's profit margins have trended up. However, they are starting to go a bit sideways.

Nvidia has gone from Wall Street's favorite stock to one of its most heavily sold stocks in just a few weeks. Shares have dropped about 22% over the past month, and Wednesday's session was ugly. The stock closed at $186.24, down nearly 7% on the day, as a broad sell-off hit the chip sector hard. AMD fell more than 17% and Broadcom dropped more than 10%.

Jim Cramer, the host of CNBC's Mad Money, spent part of his Wednesday program making the case that now is the time to buy. His argument rests on valuation: "This is the cheapest multiple on Nvidia in about a decade. We're at 16.5 now." He said investors are writing off a company he believes remains the dominant force in artificial intelligence infrastructure, 24/7 Wall St. reported.

What sparked the Nvidia selloff

The slide started in late September. At that point, Nvidia's shares sat at about 17 times forward earnings, a level not seen since January 2015.

The stock's 15-year average is roughly 30 times. The discount was real, but sellers kept coming anyway.

The trigger on Wednesday appears to have been a mix of concerns: worries about AI regulation, questions over whether hyperscalers will keep spending at the pace Nvidia needs, and rotation out of high-multiple tech names. The selloff was broad enough to drag down the entire chip sector, not just Nvidia.

Nvidia's fundamentals tell a different story

The business results themselves have been hard to fault. In its fiscal second quarter, Nvidia posted revenue of $96.2 billion, up sharply from a year earlier. Data center revenue came in at $89 billion, a 117% jump. Earnings of $2.22 a share beat the $2.09 consensus estimate. The company guided for fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, a figure that left some investors expecting more, according to Nvidia.

The company has also been using its cash aggressively. Nvidia repurchased about $39.8 billion worth of its own stock in the first half of fiscal 2027, and it still had $99 billion left on its buyback authorization at the end of the second quarter. Total buyback capacity, including a new tranche approved in late September, now stands at $235 billion, Cramer noted on X.

Cash on the balance sheet stood at $56.6 billion. Supply commitments have more than doubled, from $119 billion to $279 billion, a sign that the company is locking in future production at scale. Revenue from the roughly 50 largest frontier AI labs alone accounts for about $50 billion of that pipeline, the Motley Fool reported.
